transcript: Take a look at my account, wink wink. This is day nine of reviewing one of my followers games every single day until I hit 100,000 followers. Today is the turn of blunder hunter and if you want to be next, all you have to do is like this video, follow me and comment your chess.com username in the comments. So Mr. Blunder, I had a look at your account and I have to say that I have pinpointed a few weaknesses in your play and one major weakness, which is the opening phase of the game. You are playing this kind of odd weird system with G3. Almost no matter what your opponent plays, you're fianchettoing this bishop and this is not good because you can't always fianchetto this bishop. In this case, there's no point in doing that. After you bring the bishop here, it is going to bite on granite like this. This pawn is always going to be defended and because you have blocked your C pawn, you can't even try to open up this diagonal for the bishop, which is usually one of the main ideas, for example in the Catalan. And as you can see from the opening, black is already slightly better. You haven't blundered anything. It's just positionally and strategically unsound. You keep going with this unusual setup. I see that you like bringing this knight to E2, but of course the knight belongs on F3, where at least it can control some of the center and this pawn. It doesn't matter that you leave this open for the bishop. The bishop is not seeing anything anyway. The game continues and after a while we get to this point where black targets your B pawn. Now this is another moment that tells me that you need to work on your positional understanding. You play your rook to B1 and this seems to make sense, but you are placing a rook on the same diagonal of this bishop and in the future you will always have troubles pushing the C pawn and you're also forcing this powerful piece to be stranded defending a pawn. So what would have been better here? Well, knight to A4, a more active move. You're attacking the queen, defending the pawn and a lot of people get scared because it seems like the queen can attack the knight in these scenarios, but now you can play C3. The queen is defending the knight and you're creating a pawn chain in the center. Black has no easy way to target this pawn. If they try to make way for the B pawn, now you can push your own B pawn like this. And now we're starting to come up with some plans. If black pushes this knight away, this is actually a mistake, a positional mistake, because you gain a very strong outpost. And if this trade happens, you gain a passed pawn. I'm not saying that you should see all that from this position, but you have to look for more active moves, especially in a position where most of your pieces are not doing anything. But what I really want you take away from this is the fact that all of these issues came from the opening.
